nameStory: Lungwort gets its name from medieval herbalists who believed its spotted leaves looked like diseased lungs, following the ancient "doctrine of signatures" that said plants resembling body parts could cure ailments of those organs. They used it to treat respiratory problems, though we now know the lung-like appearance is just a lovely coincidence of nature's artistry.
description: Lungwort is a low-growing perennial herb that forms neat clumps about 8-12 inches tall and wide. Its most striking feature is the beautifully spotted leaves - dark green ovals decorated with silvery-white patches that look like they've been splattered with moonlight. In early spring, clusters of small funnel-shaped flowers emerge, starting pink and gradually turning blue as they age, creating a charming two-toned display.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Soft, fuzzy oval leaves covered in distinctive silvery-white spots on dark green background - run your fingers over them and they feel like velvet with a slightly rough texture from tiny hairs

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small trumpet-shaped flowers in drooping clusters that start pink in bud and turn bright blue when fully open - often both colors appear on the same plant at once

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms low, spreading clumps that stay close to the ground, rarely exceeding one foot in height, with leaves emerging directly from underground stems

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Leaves are evergreen and persist through winter, though they may look weathered - fresh spotted foliage emerges in spring alongside the flowers

habitat: Lungwort thrives in shaded woodland gardens and naturalized areas with rich, moist soil. While not native to New England, it has escaped cultivation and can occasionally be found in partially shaded spots near old homesteads or abandoned gardens. It prefers the dappled light under deciduous trees where the soil stays consistently moist but not waterlogged.

seasonality.spring: The magic happens in early spring when pink buds open into blue flowers, creating a delightful two-toned display that lasts for several weeks. Fresh spotted leaves emerge alongside the blooms.
seasonality.summer: Flowers fade but the stunning spotted foliage takes center stage, forming attractive ground-covering clumps in shaded areas.
seasonality.fall: Leaves remain green and spotted, though they may look slightly tired - lungwort doesn't put on a fall color show but stays recognizable.
seasonality.winter: The spotted leaves persist through winter, though they may appear somewhat weathered and flattened under snow - still identifiable by their distinctive markings.

funFact: Lungwort flowers are nature's mood rings - they contain special pigments that change color as the flower ages and the pH inside the petals shifts, starting pink when acidic and turning blue as they become more alkaline!
confusionNotes: The spotted leaves make lungwort pretty unmistakable, but it might be confused with other members of the borage family when not in bloom. Look for the distinctive silvery spots and soft, fuzzy texture - no other common garden plant has quite the same moonlight-splattered appearance.
contextualKnowledge: Though called "lungwort," this plant is completely unrelated to the lung lichens that also bear this name. It's a garden escapee rather than a true New England native, originally brought over from Europe by early settlers who valued it for both medicine and ornamental beauty.
compareHints: Lungwort differs from its close relative Bethlehem-sage by having more rounded, less pointed leaves and smaller, less showy spots. While both have the characteristic spotted foliage and color-changing flowers, common lungwort's spots tend to be more scattered and less defined than the bold white blotches of Bethlehem-sage.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Bethlehem-sage differs from common lungwort primarily in its leaf spots - Bethlehem-sage has silvery spots that merge and flow together like spilled milk, while common lungwort has distinct, separate round spots.
